prompt: Why does adding up item estimates give a date that is too early? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Estimates of work leave out the waiting
choices.why: Right. Most of an item's time was waiting.

choices.text: Percentiles do not add up
choices.why: Right. Thirty medians summed is very unlikely to be met.

choices.text: Developers always pad their estimates
choices.why: Padding would push the date later, not earlier.

choices.text: It ignores how work runs in parallel and depends on throughput
choices.why: Right. The date depends on throughput, Little's law.

prompt: Each of 5 independent items has a 50% chance of finishing within its estimate. What is the chance, in percent, that all 5 do? Answer to one decimal place.
What single number already contains all the waiting, parallel work and interruptions of a team?

choices.text: The sum of its story points
choices.why: Points are estimates; they contain none of the waiting.

choices.text: Its headcount
choices.why: Headcount says nothing about what actually got done.

choices.text: Items finished per day
choices.why: Right. Daily throughput is the history a forecast learns from.

choices.text: The length of its sprint
choices.why: A sprint length is a rhythm, not a measurement.

prompt: Put the steps of a Monte Carlo forecast in order.
items: record the throughput of every day in a recent period
draw days from it at random to make one possible future
read percentiles off the spread of results

prompt: Why do weekends appear in the history as zeros?

choices.text: Because the future will have weekends too
choices.why: Right. Calendar days in, calendar days out.

choices.text: Because the program cannot read Saturdays
choices.why: It reads every day the same way.

choices.text: To make the forecast more pessimistic on purpose
choices.why: They are there because they happened, not to bias anything.

choices.text: Because the team deploys on weekends
choices.why: Nothing merged on weekends; that is why they are zero.

prompt: Which assumption does the method make about consecutive days?

choices.text: That they always have the same throughput
choices.why: The whole point is that they vary.

choices.text: That a good day is followed by a bad one
choices.why: It assumes no pattern at all between days.

choices.text: That weekends are skipped
choices.why: Weekends are in the history as zeros.

choices.text: That they are independent
choices.why: Right. Clusters of bad days break this assumption.

prompt: Why do the lesson's programs fix the random seed?

choices.text: To make the forecast more accurate
choices.why: A seed changes nothing about accuracy.

choices.text: So your runs match the lesson's
choices.why: Right. Without it the answers wobble by an item or a day.

choices.text: Because Python requires a seed
choices.why: It does not; it picks one by itself.

choices.text: To hide the randomness from stakeholders
choices.why: The randomness is the method, and nothing to hide.

prompt: howmany.py 31 says 85% of runs finished at least how many items?
For a question about how many items, why do the percentiles count up from the bottom?

choices.text: Because larger numbers are less reliable
choices.why: Reliability is not the reason; the direction of the risk is.

choices.text: Because the histogram is drawn that way
choices.why: The drawing follows the question, not the reverse.

choices.text: Most futures reach a safe promise
choices.why: Right. 85% of futures finished at least 29.

choices.text: Because the median is always at the bottom
choices.why: The median is in the middle by definition.

prompt: The history holds 51 items in 45 days. At that average rate, how many items do 31 days give, to the nearest whole number?
A tech lead tells a stakeholder "we could do 40 in October", reading the high end of the histogram. What is wrong?

choices.text: Fewer than a quarter of futures reached 40
choices.why: Right. A number from the top is a hope, not a promise.

choices.text: 40 is impossible
choices.why: It happened in about a fifth of the futures.

choices.text: Forecasts should never mention a number
choices.why: They should; with its probability.

choices.text: The median is 40
choices.why: The median is 35.

prompt: Whose decision is how much risk to take on an October forecast?

choices.text: The team's, by choosing which percentile to quote
choices.why: The team offers the options; it should not hide the choice.

choices.text: The program's, which picks the 85th
choices.why: The program prints several; people choose.

choices.text: Nobody's; risk cannot be chosen
choices.why: It can, once the forecast is given as a spread.

choices.text: The stakeholder's
choices.why: Right. 29 at 85%, 35 at even odds: they choose.

prompt: when.py says 85% of runs finished by Sunday 1 November. What should the stakeholder be told?

choices.text: Done on Sunday 1 November
choices.why: Nothing finishes on weekends; those runs ended on Friday.

choices.text: 85% likely by the end of October
choices.why: Right. Runs ending on Sunday finished on Friday 30 October.

choices.text: Certainly by 1 November
choices.why: 85% is not certainty; 15% of futures finished later.

choices.text: On 27 October
choices.why: That is the median: even odds.

prompt: Sixty items took twice as long as thirty, but the median-to-95th gap grew only from eight days to twelve. Why?

choices.text: Because the program caps the spread
choices.why: Nothing caps it.

choices.text: Because later months are more predictable
choices.why: The simulation draws from the same history either way.

choices.text: More days let good and bad days even out
choices.why: Right. Uncertainty grows more slowly than the work.

choices.text: Because sixty items are smaller than thirty
choices.why: Items are drawn as items; their size is not in the model.

prompt: For 30 items the median finish is 27 October and the 95th percentile 4 November. How many days apart are they?
For a question about when, the percentiles count from the ___ end of the results.
Learning from June and July instead of late August and September, how many items does the 85% October forecast drop by?
Why should the history window not span the Billing team's 3 August change?

choices.text: The old rules describe another team
choices.why: Right. One policy only, and leave out the weeks right after a change.

choices.text: Because the data before August is incomplete
choices.why: They are complete; they describe other rules.

choices.text: Because longer windows are always worse
choices.why: Length is fine within one policy.

choices.text: Because Monte Carlo needs exactly 45 days
choices.why: Any reasonable length works.

prompt: A team's history has a week of incidents every month, when almost nothing finishes. What does that do to a Monte Carlo forecast?

choices.text: Nothing, because those days are in the history
choices.why: They are, but drawn one at a time they rarely come together.

choices.text: It makes the forecast too pessimistic
choices.why: The opposite: clustered bad days are underestimated.

choices.text: It makes the program fail
choices.why: It runs; the result is just optimistic.

choices.text: Bad runs are underestimated
choices.why: Right. Quote a higher percentile, such as the 95th.

prompt: Why re-run the forecast every week?

choices.text: Because the seed changes each week
choices.why: The seed is fixed; the history is what changes.

choices.text: New history and fewer items left; drift shows trouble
choices.why: Right. A sliding 85% date warns weeks before a deadline.

choices.text: Because stakeholders forget the date
choices.why: Memory is not the reason.

choices.text: Because a forecast is only valid for seven days by law
choices.why: No such rule.

prompt: Match each question to the program that answers it and how its percentiles are read.

pairs.right: howmany.py, counting up from the low end

pairs.left: when will these 30 items be done?
pairs.right: when.py, counting from the early end

prompt: A Monte Carlo forecast for thirty items says 85% by 30 October. Three weeks later, with history added, it says 85% by 13 November. What is the right reading?

choices.text: The first forecast was a mistake and should be hidden
choices.why: It was right for the history it had; hiding it hides the signal.

choices.text: The program is unreliable
choices.why: It did what it should; the input changed.

choices.text: Something slowed down; ask what
choices.why: Right. The drift is information, weeks before the deadline.

choices.text: The team should work weekends to recover the date
choices.why: That trades the date for the people, lesson 8.
